quote: Inwiefern verbürgt mein Vollständigkeitsaxiom die eindeutige [?] deutige Bestimmtheit der Begriffe (des System aller Zahlen, der Geometrie etc.)?
english: To what extent does my completeness axiom guarantee the unique determinateness of the concepts (of the system of all numbers, of geometry, etc.)?
topic: Miscellaneous notes: improbable states in molecular physics, an argument against theologians that logical definition rather than etymology matters, whether a complete axiom system determines its concepts uniquely (categoricity), and Kronecker's program as an axiomatic demand for a non-Archimedean theory of equations.

triage.modern_statement: Hilbert is asking whether his completeness axiom (Vollständigkeitsaxiom) makes his axiom systems categorical. The axiom first appeared in 'Über den Zahlbegriff' (1899/1900) for the real numbers and was added to the Grundlagen der Geometrie from the 2nd edition on. It is a maximality condition: the model cannot be extended to a larger structure that still satisfies the other axioms. In modern terms the question is whether every model of the axioms for the real numbers (an Archimedean ordered field plus completeness), or of Hilbert's full axioms for Euclidean geometry, is isomorphic to every other model. A further question is what kind of logic this needs. The axiom quantifies over extensions or subsets, so it is second-order and cannot be stated as a single first-order sentence.
triage.answered_by: Huntington (1902, with the notion of 'absolute definiteness') and Veblen (1904, who coined the term 'categorical') stated and proved categoricity for full axiom systems of the reals and of geometry. Veblen believed in 1904 that any axiom system containing Hilbert's completeness axiom must be categorical. Under the standard (second-order) reading the answer is yes: Hilbert's axioms for the reals and for Euclidean geometry are categorical, so the concepts are fixed up to isomorphism. Later logic clarified the limits. Löwenheim (1915) and Skolem (c. 1920) showed that no first-order theory with an infinite model is categorical, because it has models of other cardinalities. This is why the completeness axiom only gives uniqueness when read as second-order, and why second-order logic then loses the completeness and compactness theorems. Recent historical work (e.g. 'Hilbert on categoricity and completeness') finds that Hilbert himself implied but never proved that his axioms are categorical. That supports reading this note as a question he left open.

evidence.claim: Veblen (1904) named the property that all models are isomorphic 'categoricity'. Hilbert introduced the completeness axiom in 'Über den Zahlbegriff' (1899/1900) and used a similar axiom in later editions of the Grundlagen. The source says the axiom implies categoricity.

Huntington (1902) used 'absolute definiteness' as categoricity. Veblen (1904) called a system of twelve axioms 'categorical' and believed that every axiom system containing Hilbert's completeness axiom must be categorical.
Hilbert implied but did not try to prove that his axiom systems are categorical, and did not treat categoricity as a general requirement. The term was coined by Veblen (1904).
Because second-order logic can characterize the natural numbers and the ordered field of reals, the Completeness and Compactness theorems fail for it, as do Löwenheim–Skolem-type results.
The Löwenheim–Skolem theorem was first proved by Löwenheim in 1915, with a more general proof by Skolem around 1920. It does not hold in second-order logic.
The completeness axiom for geometry plays a role comparable to the induction axiom for arithmetic. Veblen proposed a geometry axiom system in 1904.

triage.why: The note asks whether the completeness axiom guarantees 'eindeutige Bestimmtheit' of the number system and of geometry. That is exactly the categoricity question. Huntington (1902) and Veblen (1904) took it up shortly afterwards. It was settled mathematically: the systems are categorical under the second-order reading, and Löwenheim–Skolem shows a first-order version cannot be categorical. It is not one of the 23 problems. It is a well-known episode in the history of logic. The foundational and historical debate continues (e.g. 'Hilbert on categoricity and completeness', and work on second-order versus first-order semantics), but that is discussion of a settled result, not an open problem, which is why active_today is 'no'. The diary page itself is undated, so I can't tell exactly how it relates in time to Huntington's and Veblen's papers.
